h1:
Sa Kaeo & Prachinburi: 3 Days, 2 Nights
Forests and Khmer Temples in Eastern Thailand
intro: Prachinburi and Sa Kaeo are next-door neighbours linked by a single road (Highway 33, the Suwannason road), so it's easy to roll them into one trip. You start in Prachinburi, which is all about forests, waterfalls, ancient trees, and century-old buildings, then drift east into Sa Kaeo with its Pang Sida forest, limestone hills, and thousand-year-old Khmer temples. We've laid this out as a relaxed 3 days and 2 nights — only a few dozen kilometres of driving each day, with real time to walk in the forest and explore the temples on foot.

blocks.html: The nice thing about pairing these two provinces is that the sights never feel repetitive. Prachinburi leans into forests, herbal medicine, and antiquities, while Sa Kaeo is more about geology, temples, and the border. Stitch them together and you get a trip where you walk through forest in the morning, look at old buildings in the afternoon, relax by the water in the evening, and stand in front of thousand-year-old stone temples the next day. A private car is by far the easiest way to do all of this, since many of the stops are well outside town and public transport doesn't reach them.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: This trip is built around driving yourself. From Bangkok, take the motorway plus Highway 33 and you'll reach Prachinburi in about two and a half hours. If you don't have a car, rent one in Bangkok before you leave — rental options inside these provinces are limited. Fill up the tank before heading into the national park areas.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Prachinburi: forest, waterfalls, century-old buildings

blocks.html: Day one is for ticking off Prachinburi's highlights. Spend the cooler morning hours in nature, then head into town in the afternoon for the old buildings. For the night you can stay in Prachinburi town or out toward Kabin Buri — it depends on which way you'll drive into Sa Kaeo the next day.

items.activity: Leave Bangkok, head for Prachinburi
items.note: Motorway + Highway 33, about 2.5 hours. You can stop for breakfast along the way.

items.activity: Wat Ton Pho Si Maha Phot, Si Maha Phot district
items.note: Believed to be the oldest bodhi tree in Thailand, with a trunk around 20 metres in circumference, shading the whole courtyard. Free entry.

items.activity: Sa Morakot historical site (ancient city of Si Mahosot)
items.note: A pair of Buddha footprints carved into laterite, alongside an ancient pond. Right near the bodhi tree — just a few minutes' drive further.

items.activity: Lunch in Prachinburi town
items.note: Boat noodles, rice-and-curry shops, or a riverside spot along the Bang Pakong — plenty of choices.

items.activity: Chao Phraya Abhaibhubejhr building + herbal museum
items.note: A European-style building over 100 years old, great for photos, with an Abhaibhubejhr herbal shop for souvenirs.

items.activity: Waterfall walk / bamboo rafting around Kabin Buri (seasonal)
items.note: Plenty of water in the rainy season — you can soak in the falls. In the dry season the water runs low, so swap in a riverside cafe instead.

items.activity: Check in + dinner in town
items.note: Stay in Prachinburi or Kabin Buri, depending on which way you'll head into Sa Kaeo tomorrow.

blocks.title: About the waterfalls
blocks.html: Waterfalls and bamboo rafting around Prachinburi and Sa Kaeo depend heavily on the season. The best stretch is late rainy season into early cool season (September–December). In the dry season (March–May) the water is often low or gone. Plan with that in mind — if you go in the dry season, focus on temples and caves rather than waterfalls.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Crossing into Sa Kaeo: Pang Sida forest and Khao Chakan

blocks.html: Today is the cross-province day, driving from Prachinburi into Sa Kaeo. The headliner is Pang Sida National Park, which actually straddles both provinces, with waterfalls and butterfly-watching spots (butterflies peak around May–July). In the afternoon you drop down to Khao Chakan, a limestone hill with caves and swarms of bats that fly out at dusk. Tonight you move into Sa Kaeo town to get set for a final day of temples.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Prachinburi → Sa Kaeo — forest and limestone hills

items.activity: Set off for Pang Sida National Park
items.note: The main entrance is on the Sa Kaeo side, with a winding mountain road. Park entry is around 40 THB for Thai adults.

items.activity: Pang Sida Waterfall + nature trail
items.note: The falls are near the headquarters and not a long walk. The water is strong and lovely in the rainy season, and there are plenty of butterflies around May–July.

items.activity: Picnic lunch / park canteen
items.note: Food inside the park is limited, so it's best to bring water and snacks in the car.

items.activity: Drive down toward Khao Chakan
items.note: About an hour from Pang Sida to Khao Chakan, passing through Sa Kaeo town.

items.activity: Wat Tham Khao Chakan + Tham Khao Thalu cave
items.note: Climb the stairs to see the cave and the views at Khao Thalu. Lots of monkeys, so watch any food in your hands.

items.activity: Wait for the bats to fly out of the cave (if the timing works)
items.note: At dusk the bats stream out in a long ribbon — a sight plenty of people come specifically to wait for.

items.activity: Into Sa Kaeo town, check in + dinner
items.note: Stay in Sa Kaeo town or Aranyaprathet, depending on your Day 3 plan.

blocks.title: Book park accommodation ahead
blocks.html: If you want to sleep over in Pang Sida to stargaze and wake up for the morning butterflies, you'll need to book a cabin or campsite through the national park reservation system (nps.dnp.go.th) in advance. These fill up fast on long weekends. If you'd rather not camp in the forest, just stay in town as this plan suggests.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Sa Kaeo: Khmer temples and earthen wonders

blocks.html: The final day belongs to temples and unusual landscapes. The highlights are Sdok Kok Thom, the largest sandstone Khmer temple in Eastern Thailand, and Lalu, an eroded earth formation where the soil has been carved by rain into pillars like a miniature canyon. If you still have energy, you can add Khao Noi Si Chomphu temple before looping back to Bangkok.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Sa Kaeo — Khmer temples and Lalu

items.activity: Sdok Kok Thom temple, Khok Sung district
items.note: An 11th-century Khmer temple, beautifully restored, with an information centre that explains its history. Free entry — go early before the sun gets harsh.

items.activity: Lalu, Ta Phraya district
items.note: Oddly shaped earth pillars spread across a wide area. Local homestays and villagers run vehicle tours — a few hundred THB per vehicle.

items.activity: Lunch around Aranyaprathet
items.note: Try local Thai–Khmer food, such as Khmer-style noodles, or grab a bite at the market.

items.activity: Khao Noi Si Chomphu temple, Aranyaprathet district (optional)
items.note: A brick temple on a low hill — climb the stairs for views all around. One of the province's older historical sites.

items.activity: Rong Kluea Market for souvenirs (optional)
items.note: A large border market selling secondhand goods and cheap finds. Trading conditions vary from one period to another, so check before you go.

items.activity: Head back to Bangkok
items.note: From Aranyaprathet back to Bangkok is about 3 to 3.5 hours — allow extra for evening traffic.

blocks.title: About the border and crossing over
blocks.html: This plan stays entirely on the Thai side and doesn't take you across into Cambodia. Spots like Rong Kluea Market and the Khlong Luek–Poipet checkpoint sit right on the border, where opening hours and the trading atmosphere shift over time. If you do plan to cross over or visit the border market, always check the latest situation, the checkpoint's opening hours, and the documents you'll need (passport / border pass) with the relevant authorities before you actually go.

blocks.text: Adjusting the plan to your time

items: Only 2 days — drop the Kabin Buri waterfall and merge Days 1 and 2: cover Prachinburi in the morning, cross into Pang Sida in the afternoon, sleep in Sa Kaeo, then hit the temples on the second day.
Travelling with kids — focus on the Si Maha Phot bodhi tree, the Abhaibhubejhr building, Khao Chakan (monkeys and bats), and Lalu, and cut back on the heavier forest walks.
History buffs — add a temple day: a full day for Sdok Kok Thom + Khao Noi Si Chomphu + the museums in town.
Dry season — shift the focus to temples and caves, since many of the waterfalls run low.

blocks.html: This trip is two nights: the first on the Prachinburi / Kabin Buri side, the second on the Sa Kaeo side (in town or Aranyaprathet). Both sides have everything from riverside resorts and in-town hotels to homestays near Lalu, with prices running from the high hundreds to around a thousand-plus THB a night. On long weekends you'll want to book ahead, especially the places near the national parks, which have only a limited number of rooms.

items.name: Night 1: Prachinburi / Kabin Buri side
items.blurb: A riverside resort or in-town hotel, handy for driving into Pang Sida the next day.

items.name: Night 2: Sa Kaeo town / Aranyaprathet
items.blurb: Close to the temple route and Lalu, and ready for the drive back to Bangkok on the last day.

faq.q: How many days do you need for Sa Kaeo and Prachinburi?
faq.a: Three days and two nights is just right — enough to take in Prachinburi's forests, Pang Sida, and the Khmer temples in Sa Kaeo without rushing. You can do it in 2 days, but you'll have to cut some of the waterfalls and drive more each day.

faq.q: Is it far to drive from Prachinburi to Sa Kaeo?
faq.a: Not far. The two provinces sit on the same road, Highway 33 (Suwannason). From Prachinburi town to Sa Kaeo town is about an hour and a half. The individual sights are scattered off the main road, though, so a private car is by far the easiest way to get around.

faq.q: When is the best time to do this trip?
faq.a: Late rainy season into early cool season (September–December), when the waterfalls still have water and the weather is comfortably cool. If you want to see the butterflies at Pang Sida, come around May–July. In the dry season the waterfalls tend to be low, so focus on temples and caves instead.

faq.q: Do you have to cross into Cambodia?
faq.a: No. This plan stays entirely on the Thai side. Spots like Rong Kluea Market and the Khlong Luek checkpoint sit on the border — if you want to stop by or cross over, check the latest situation, the checkpoint hours, and the required documents with the relevant authorities before you actually go.

faq.q: Do you have to stay overnight in the forest to visit Pang Sida?
faq.a: Not necessarily. This plan has you visiting Pang Sida as a day trip and returning to town to sleep. But if you want to stargaze and wake up for the morning butterflies, you can book a cabin or campsite through the national park system in advance.
